Comment: Only in possessed nouns.

Is there ergative alignment of flagging on second person pronouns?
Is there ergative alignment of flagging on third person pronouns?
Comment: The ergative case is named "relative case" in the source.

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging on full NPs?
Comment: Full NPs that refer to first or second person participants are flagged with locative case, instead of absolutive or ergative case (p. 731).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the imperfective aspect?
Comment: Verbs are not obligatorily marked for aspect. No mention nor evidence of an aspect-based split in case marking. See, for instance, the clause with an imperfective interpretation in (3).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the perfective aspect?
Comment: Verbs are not obligatorily marked for aspect. No mention nor evidence of an aspect-based split in case marking. See, for instance, the clause with a perfective interpretation in (9).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the past tense?
Comment: Verbs are not obligatorily marked for past tense. No mention nor evidence of a tense-based split in case marking. See in example (21) a clause with a past-tense reading, an absolutive argument aipa-ni ('partner-ABS') and an ergative argument aipa-an ('partner-ERG').

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in non-past tenses?
Comment: Verbs are not obligatorily marked for non-past tense. No mention nor evidence of a tense-based split in case marking. See an example with a present-tense reading and ergative alignment in (1).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the indicative mood?
Comment: No mention nor evidence of a mood-based split in case marking. See example (9).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in non-indicative moods?
Comment: No mention nor evidence of a mood-based split in case marking. See example (39) in interrogative mood.

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the realis status?
Comment: No mention nor evidence of a split in case marking based on the realis-irrealis distinction. See example (9).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the irrealis status?
Comment: No mention nor evidence of a split in case marking based on the realis-irrealis distinction. Examples in the source do not offer evidence of such a split in negated clauses, in the future tense or in the optative mood.

Comment: See example (9).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the context of a non-agentive A?
Comment: See examples (3) in p. 732 and (1) in p. 737.

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the context of a topical A?
Comment: The grammar exhaustively describes case marking and alingments in the language but there is no mention nor evidence of a split based on the topicality of the A argument.

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the context of a non-topical A?
Comment: The grammar exhaustively describes case marking and alingments in the language but there is no mention nor evidence of a split based on the topicality of the A argument.

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the context of an animate A?
Comment: See example (9).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in the context of an inanimate A?
Comment: See example (209b).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in main clauses?
Comment: See example (9).

Feature: Is there ergative alignment of flagging in non-main clauses?
Comment: In nominal clauses S/A arguments take the ergative marker while the P argument is unmarked (accusative alignment). In relative clauses, when an A or P argument is relativized, the other core argument that remains inside the relative clause takes the ergative marker. When an oblique argument is relativized, the S/A argument inside the relative clause takes the ergative marker (accusative alignment).

Feature: Is ergative alignment of flagging conditioned by any other factor?
Comment: There is a number-based split: the distinction between absolutive and ergative only occurs in the third person singular, while they are not marked in the dual and plural numbers. Another split occurs if the P argument "is backgrounded, is indefinite or only partly affected": P takes ablative case while the A argument takes absolutive case (forming an accusative alignment). This is considered an antipassivization by the source, but the verb does not take an antipassive marker in this context.
